HomeIntro.title: A map built to make charging effortless
HomeIntro.body1: ma-borne-electrique.com lists available EV charging stations across Europe and beyond, using open data from Open Charge Map and network operators. Whether you're looking for a station near home, on a road trip, or in a city you're just visiting, the map shows its location, connector type, and charging power at a glance, with no account and no app to install.
HomeIntro.body2: Slow charging at home, accelerated charging in town, or fast charging on the motorway: every trip has different needs. Our practical guides cover Type 2, CCS, and CHAdeMO connectors, their power output and real-world charging times, as well as range, price, and incentives for buying an electric car, so you can choose the right station and the right vehicle with confidence.

Faq.title: Before you head out to charge
Faq.q1: Is the station data up to date?
Faq.a1: The map relies on Open Charge Map, a collaborative database fed by operators and the community. Real-time availability depends on what each operator publishes; if in doubt, check the status on site or via the operator's app.
Faq.a2: Yes, searching for and locating stations on ma-borne-electrique.com is completely free. The cost of charging depends on the station operator, not on our service.
Faq.q3: What's the difference between slow, fast, and rapid charging?
Faq.a3: In short: slow (up to 22 kW AC) for a charge lasting several hours, fast (22 kW) for a few hours, and rapid (50 kW and above, DC) to regain good range in 20 to 40 minutes. The details are explained in our connector guide.
Faq.q4: How much does it cost to charge an electric car?
Faq.a4: At home, expect around €2 to €4 per 100 km depending on your electricity rate, versus €10 to €20 on a public rapid charger. Charging at home or at work stays roughly 3 to 5 times cheaper than rapid charging on the road. Our electric car guide breaks down the cost by charging type.
Faq.q5: What range can I expect from an electric car today?
Faq.a5: Most recent models offer between 300 and 500 km of WLTP range, with city cars closer to 250-350 km and some premium saloons above 600 km. Real-world range is typically 10 to 20% lower than the WLTP figure in everyday driving.

ConnectorGuide.title: Type 2, CCS, CHAdeMO: which connector for your electric vehicle?
ConnectorGuide.intro: Every charging station offers one or more connector types, each tied to a maximum power output. Here's how to make sense of it before you plug in.
ConnectorGuide.acDcBody: A charging station delivers either alternating current (AC) or direct current (DC), and this choice directly determines how fast your car can charge. AC charging passes through the vehicle's onboard charger, a built-in component that converts grid power into current the battery can use; this limits the real power output, typically between 3.7 and 22 kW, on Type 2 connectors (IEC 62196 standard). DC charging bypasses the onboard charger entirely: the charger sits inside the station itself and feeds the battery directly, allowing much higher power, from 50 to 350 kW on rapid chargers, using Combo CCS or CHAdeMO connectors. In short: AC suits slow charging at home or work, while DC is reserved for quick top-ups on the road.
ConnectorGuide.connector1Time: 24 to 40 h for a full charge
ConnectorGuide.connector2Usage: Charging at home, at work, on the street
ConnectorGuide.connector2Time: 4 to 10 h depending on power and battery
ConnectorGuide.connector3Usage: Rapid charging on motorways and urban hubs
ConnectorGuide.connector4Usage: Rapid charging, mostly older Japanese vehicles
ConnectorGuide.tableFootnote: Charging times are approximate: they depend on battery capacity, its temperature, and the vehicle's onboard charger.
ConnectorGuide.choose1Body: a Type 2 station at home or at work (7 to 22 kW) is more than enough for an overnight charge or during working hours.
ConnectorGuide.choose2Body: favour a rapid Combo CCS station (50 kW and above) on motorway routes to keep your stop short.
ConnectorGuide.choose3Body: check CHAdeMO compatibility, a standard still found on some models but increasingly rare on new stations.
ConnectorGuide.homeChargingBody: For daily use, a reinforced socket (up to 3.2 kW) or, better, a wallbox (7 to 22 kW) installed by a professional remains the most economical and fastest solution. A 7 kW wallbox charges a 50 kWh battery in 7 to 8 hours: more than enough for an overnight charge, and compatible with most electric cars on the market.
ConnectorGuide.costHeading: How much does charging cost by connector type?
ConnectorGuide.costBody: What you pay to charge depends mainly on where you charge, since each public network sets its own prices in a deregulated charging market. At home, the rate follows your household electricity plan: expect around €0.15 to €0.25/kWh off-peak, less if your contract includes an off-peak/peak-hours option. On a public Type 2 station, 2026 rates typically run €0.30 to €0.50/kWh. On a rapid DC station (Combo CCS) while on the road, expect €0.40 to €0.70/kWh, with the higher price reflecting the speed of the charge. For a vehicle averaging 17 kWh/100 km, that works out to between €2.50 and €12 per 100 km depending on where you charge, a gap that makes charging at home or at work worth prioritizing whenever possible.
ConnectorGuide.relatedGuideBox: Still unsure which model or range you need? Check our <link>complete electric car guide</link>.
ConnectorGuide.ctaBox: Ready to find a station compatible with your vehicle? <link>Check the charging map</link>.
ConnectorGuide.imageAlt: Close-up of a CCS Combo charging connector
ConnectorGuide.faq1Q: What's the difference between AC and DC charging?
ConnectorGuide.faq1A: AC charging runs through the vehicle's onboard charger and is generally capped between 3.7 and 22kW, while DC charging feeds the battery directly through an external charger, at power levels from 50 to 350kW.
ConnectorGuide.faq2Q: Which connector should I use for a long-distance trip?
ConnectorGuide.faq2A: A CCS Combo fast charger is the best choice, letting you recover 20 to 80% battery in 20 to 40 minutes.
ConnectorGuide.faq3Q: How long does charging take with a home wallbox?
ConnectorGuide.faq3A: A 7kW wallbox charges a 50kWh battery in 7 to 8 hours, more than enough for a full night.
ConnectorGuide.faq4Q: How much does charging cost depending on the connector type?
ConnectorGuide.faq4A: Expect around 0.15 to 0.25 euros per kWh at home outside off-peak hours, 0.30 to 0.50 euros on a public Type 2 station, and 0.40 to 0.70 euros on a fast CCS station on the road.

AProposPage.title: Making EV charging and electric cars simpler
AProposPage.missionP1: ma-borne-electrique.com is an independent website launched in 2026, with a clear mission: help electric vehicle drivers find a reliable charging station and better understand their car day to day.
AProposPage.missionP2: With charging networks, connector types, and power outputs multiplying, and clear, reliable, centralized information still hard to find, we saw that drivers struggled to make sense of it all. ma-borne-electrique.com was born from that observation.
AProposPage.coverageIntro: Our editorial line is built around two main topics:
AProposPage.coverage1Body: a real-time interactive map of charging stations across France and Europe, with power output, connector type, and availability, with no account to create and no app to install.
AProposPage.coverage2Body: real-world range, purchase and running costs, government incentives, home and public charging, and how to choose a model. We break down each topic to help you make the best choice.
AProposPage.engagementP1: ma-borne-electrique.com is an independent website. We are not affiliated with any charging network operator, car manufacturer, or financial provider. The station data shown comes from <ocm>Open Charge Map</ocm>, an open, collaborative database, and map data is provided by <osm>OpenStreetMap contributors</osm>. Our editorial content is checked before publishing.
AProposPage.engagementP2: We commit to keeping our content up to date as the market, usage, and technology evolve, and to correcting any error reported to us quickly, including on a station.
AProposPage.whoBody: ma-borne-electrique.com is an independent project run by Hugo Beignon, an application developer with a passion for electric mobility. It is a personal, non-commercial project: there is no editorial team behind the site, just one author documenting his research on the topic as carefully as possible.
AProposPage.seoP1: We believe good content answers a real question asked by a real reader. Our articles are structured to be useful first, and well ranked as a result. We never trade information quality for ranking.
AProposPage.seoP2: Our articles are organized into topic clusters: each pillar guide covers a central topic in depth, such as our <link>complete guide to charging connectors</link>, supported by satellite articles that dig into specific sub-topics. This structure keeps our information organized and consistent.
AProposPage.contactP1: Got a question, a suggestion, or spotted an error on a station? Feel free to write to us via our <link>contact form</link>. We reply within 48 business hours.
AProposPage.contactP2: Are you a journalist or blogger who wants to cite our content? Our data and analysis can be freely cited with a mention of the source and a link back to the original article.

This policy describes how we collect, use, store, and protect your data, in accordance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).

ConfidentialitePage.controllerContact: Contact: via our contact form, or by email at contact@ma-borne-electrique.com.
ConfidentialitePage.dataIntro: We collect the following personal data, depending on how you interact with our website:

This information does not pass through our servers and is not stored by the website: it is sent directly from your own mailbox.
ConfidentialitePage.dataFormLegal: Legal basis: your explicit consent (GDPR art. 6.1.a) and our legitimate interest in responding to your requests (GDPR art. 6.1.f).
ConfidentialitePage.dataAnalyticsBody: We use Google Analytics 4 to measure website traffic (pages visited, session duration, visitor origin). This service is only activated after your explicit consent, given via the cookie banner shown on your first visit. Your IP address is anonymized before processing and no personally identifiable data is shared with Google.
ConfidentialitePage.dataAnalyticsLegal: Legal basis: your explicit consent (GDPR art. 6.1.a).
ConfidentialitePage.purpose2: Improve our content and the reliability of the information shown, through anonymized statistics;

ConfidentialitePage.retention2: Cookie consent preference: kept for 12 months in your browser.
ConfidentialitePage.retention3: Analytics data: kept for 13 months maximum.
ConfidentialitePage.recipientsBody: Your personal data is never sold to third parties. It may be shared with our technical service providers (our host, Hostinger, and, if you have given your consent, Google Analytics for traffic measurement) strictly for the performance of their services, which are bound by confidentiality obligations. Where data is transferred outside the European Union (e.g. Google, a US company), appropriate safeguards are in place (European Commission standard contractual clauses).

ConfidentialitePage.right1: Right of access (GDPR art. 15): obtain confirmation that your data is processed and request a copy.
ConfidentialitePage.right2: Right to rectification (GDPR art. 16): have inaccurate data about you corrected.
ConfidentialitePage.right3: Right to erasure (GDPR art. 17): request deletion of your data, subject to our legal obligations.
ConfidentialitePage.right4: Right to restriction (GDPR art. 18): request the temporary suspension of processing.
ConfidentialitePage.right5: Right to object (GDPR art. 21): object to processing based on our legitimate interest.

EVGuide.title: Electric car: the complete guide (range, price, charging, incentives)
EVGuide.intro: Real-world range, purchase and running costs, government incentives, and charging options: here's everything you need to know before switching to an electric car, or to get more out of the one you already have.
EVGuide.howItWorksHeading: How does an electric car work
EVGuide.howItWorksBody: An electric car replaces the combustion engine with one or more electric motors, powered by a rechargeable lithium-ion battery. There's no traditional gearbox, no clutch, no exhaust: driving is quieter, smoother, and mechanical maintenance drops by roughly 30 to 40% compared with an equivalent combustion vehicle, since there's no oil change, timing belt, or clutch to replace.
EVGuide.rangeHeading: What range can you expect from an electric car?
EVGuide.rangeIntro: The range advertised by manufacturers follows the WLTP cycle, measured under standardised conditions. In real-world use, expect around 10 to 20% less, more still in cold weather or on the motorway.
EVGuide.rangeFootnote: Approximate figures observed on recent models (2024-2026), for guidance only.
EVGuide.rangeFactorsBody: Outside temperature (cold can cut range by 20 to 30%), speed (driving at 130 km/h uses noticeably more energy than at 90 km/h), driving style, load, and use of air conditioning or heating all strongly affect real-world range. Anticipating traffic and eco-driving can recover 10 to 15% of range in everyday use.
EVGuide.priceHeading: Purchase and running costs: electric vs combustion
EVGuide.priceIntro: Upfront, an electric car remains on average 20 to 40% more expensive than an equivalent combustion model. That gap narrows sharply in use thanks to lower charging and maintenance costs.
EVGuide.priceFootnote: Indicative 2026 figures, for comparison purposes. They vary by model, annual mileage, and charging method used.
EVGuide.aidsHeading: Grants and incentives for buying an electric car
EVGuide.aidsBody: Many European countries, including France, Germany, and Spain, offer or have offered government and regional incentives for buying or leasing an electric car: purchase grants, scrappage schemes, or subsidised leasing for lower-income households. These schemes change frequently and vary by country, so always check the current official rules for your country before buying.
EVGuide.chargingHeading: Charging your electric car: at home, at work, on the road
EVGuide.chargingBody: Around 80 to 90% of charging happens at home or at work, on a reinforced socket or a wallbox. For longer trips, a network of rapid chargers lets you recover 20 to 80% of battery in 20 to 40 minutes. The right connector (Type 2 for everyday use, Combo CCS for rapid charging) depends on your vehicle: our <link>charging connector guide</link> covers each standard, its power, and charging time.
EVGuide.prosConsHeading: Pros and cons of the electric car
EVGuide.pros1: Lower running costs: cheaper charging and maintenance than a combustion car over time.
EVGuide.pros2: Quiet, comfortable driving, with no vibrations or petrol smell.
EVGuide.pros3: Instant acceleration thanks to torque available from a standstill.
EVGuide.pros4: Zero tailpipe emissions, and a lower overall carbon footprint over the vehicle's lifecycle in most studies.
EVGuide.cons1: Purchase price still high, despite available incentives.
EVGuide.cons2: Range and charging time to plan for on longer trips.
EVGuide.cons3: Rapid charging network still uneven depending on the region.
EVGuide.cons4: Resale value and battery ageing to keep an eye on for older models.
EVGuide.chooseHeading: How to choose your electric car based on your needs
EVGuide.choose1Body: a city car with 300 to 350 km of WLTP range is more than enough, with a full charge overnight on a wallbox.
EVGuide.choose2Body: favour a compact SUV or saloon with 400 to 500 km of range, enough boot space, and rapid charging of 100 kW or more.
EVGuide.choose3Lead: Frequent long trips and motorway driving:
EVGuide.choose3Body: choose a model with over 500 km of WLTP range and rapid charging above 150 kW, to keep stops short.
EVGuide.ctaBox: Ready to go electric? <link>Find a charging station near you</link> to plan your first trip.
EVGuide.imageAlt: A Volkswagen ID.3, an example of a compact electric car
EVGuide.faq1Q: How much real-world range should I expect from an electric car?
EVGuide.faq1A: Real-world range is usually 10 to 20% lower than the advertised WLTP figure, and the gap can widen in cold weather or on the motorway.
EVGuide.faq2Q: Is an electric car more expensive than an equivalent petrol or diesel model?
EVGuide.faq2A: Yes, upfront, typically 20 to 40% more, but the gap narrows a lot in use thanks to cheaper charging and maintenance, around 150 to 300 euros a year versus 400 to 600 euros for a combustion car.
EVGuide.faq3Q: What financial incentives exist for buying an electric car in France?
EVGuide.faq3A: The main schemes are the ecological bonus, the scrappage bonus, and social leasing for lower-income households, though their amounts and conditions change every year.
EVGuide.faq4Q: Where do most people charge their electric car?
EVGuide.faq4A: About 80 to 90% of charging happens at home or at work, on a reinforced outlet or a wallbox, while the fast-charging network is mostly used for long trips.
